Newborn nymphs of the green peach aphid (Myzus persicae) are remarkably small, with a body length at birth of only 0.0779 cm [Lb = 0.0779 cm]. This diminutive size at larviposition reflects the limited provisioning of the eggless embryo within the maternal body, a constraint common across aphid lineages. The first-instar nymph emerges fully formed and begins feeding almost immediately on the phloem sap of the host plant. At an experimental temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the first instar requires a development time of 2.42 days  to complete its stadium and moult to the second instar. This relatively brief duration is consistent with the high intrinsic growth rates observed in this polyphagous pest species. The second instar, which follows, shares an identical development time of 2.42 days  under the same thermal regime, indicating a remarkably symmetrical period of growth between these early feeding stages before any detectable increase in stadium duration emerges at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C].

Progressing through the nymphal stages under the identical constant temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the third instar exhibits a slightly longer development time of 2.46 days . This modest increase in stadium length continues into the fourth and final nymphal instar, which requires 2.58 days  to reach the imaginal moult at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. The progressive lengthening of the instar durations likely reflects the increasing metabolic demands of building a larger body, particularly as the insect approaches the critical weight necessary for metamorphosis. At the culmination of the fourth stadium, the insect moults into the winged adult form. Measurements of body length taken during these final immature stages reveal a clear growth trajectory: the second instar attains a length of 0.0834 cm , the third instar reaches 0.1062 cm , and the fourth instar achieves 0.1466 cm , each representing a substantial incremental gain over the preceding stage.

Upon completion of the nymphal period, the newly emerged imago of Myzus persicae has a body length at the imago stage of 0.1957 cm , representing a more than twofold increase from the length at birth. Under a constant thermal environment of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the total time since birth at adult emergence is 7.84 days . This relatively rapid developmental cycle is a hallmark of the species' prodigious capacity for population increase, enabling multiple overlapping generations within a single growing season. The teneral adult must first undergo cuticle sclerotization and wing expansion before becoming fully reproductive. Field records indicate that the maximum reproduction rate of adult females maintained at 20 °C was 1.66 offspring per day [Ri = 1.66 offspring per day] over a seven-day recording interval, a value that underscores the explosive outbreak potential of this aphid on favourable host plants such as Brassica oleracea.

When aphids were reared at the higher temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum reproduction rate was recorded at 1.65 offspring per day [Ri = 1.65 offspring per day] over a two-day observation period, a figure strikingly similar to the rate at 20 °C. This thermal insensitivity of the peak reproductive output between 20 °C and 25 °C suggests a broad plateau of optimal performance before heat stress begins to impair fecundity. The adult imago lifespan is relatively compressed under these warm conditions; at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the life span of an imago was measured at 5.4 days [am = 5.4 days], a short post-reproductive window that forces a highly condensed schedule of parturition. A cohort of alatiform nymphs was used to estimate a wet weight at birth of 0.00003326 grams [Wwb = 0.00003326 grams], a value assumed to be equivalent across both apterous and alate viviparous morphs, reflecting the similar maternal investment in each newborn regardless of its future wing development.

In a separate laboratory trial designed to assess biomass accumulation during early development, a group of nine-day-old aphids reared at 22 °C [T = 22 °C] and fed on young leaves of cabbage was weighed. The sample, composed of approximately 47 adults and 3 nymphs, yielded a wet weight after 9 days of 0.0006629 grams . This measurement provides a useful benchmark for comparing growth rates across different host plants or thermal conditions, as cabbage is a moderately favourable host. The ecological success of Myzus persicae is tightly linked to its ability to exploit a vast array of host species from over forty plant families, a polyphagy that buffers the aphid against local host phenology. The rapid body length increments observed from the first-instar nymph through the imago stage, combined with a high daily fecundity and a short generation time, collectively equip this species to colonise new habitats quickly and reach damaging population densities in agricultural systems worldwide.
